title: Docker in practice: build cache, image layers, stop signals & container storage
description: Each Question puts you in a concrete Docker situation. You decide what reaches the builder, when the build cache hits, what ends up in the image, how containers stop, how ports and networks connect, where data survives, and how isolated a container is.

questions.title: Can `COPY` reach a sibling directory outside the build context?
questions.description: Your project is in `/work/app`, and a private key is at `/work/private-key`. You run `docker build /work/app`, and the Dockerfile has `COPY ../private-key /run/private-key`.

options.text: Yes. `COPY` resolves paths relative to the Dockerfile on the client
No. The builder can read only the selected build context or a named context
Yes, but only when the destination is under `/run`
No. `COPY` can copy only files tracked by Git

questions.explanation: `docker build /work/app` makes `/work/app` the build context, so the builder never sees `/work/private-key`. BuildKit drops leading `../` segments, so `COPY` can't reach outside the context. To use files from another directory, pass that directory as a named context.
questions.references:
[Docker Docs: Build context](https://docs.docker.com/build/concepts/context/)

[Docker Docs: `docker image build`: accessing paths outside the context](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/image/build/#accessing-paths-outside-the-build-context)

questions.title: What happens when `.dockerignore` excludes a file that `COPY` requests?
questions.description: `.dockerignore` contains `secrets.env`, while the Dockerfile contains `COPY secrets.env /app/secrets.env`.

options.text: Docker sends the file to the builder but leaves it out of the final image
Docker replaces the file with an empty one so the build can continue
Docker drops the file from the context before sending it, so `COPY` fails with a missing source
The ignore rule applies to `ADD` but not `COPY`

questions.explanation: Docker drops ignored files before it sends the context to the builder. `secrets.env` never arrives, so `COPY` can't find it and the build fails. You can keep a file out of the context or copy it into the image, but not both.

questions.title: Which ignore file wins when a build has two?
questions.description: The context root has a `.dockerignore`. The build uses `docker/build.Dockerfile`, and `docker/build.Dockerfile.dockerignore` is next to it.

options.text: Docker merges both files, with the root file evaluated last
The Dockerfile-specific `build.Dockerfile.dockerignore` wins
Docker reads only the root `.dockerignore`
Whichever file has the newer modification time wins

questions.explanation: You can name an ignore file after a Dockerfile and put it next to that Dockerfile. When it exists, Docker uses it instead of the root `.dockerignore`. That way, each Dockerfile in a repository can have its own ignore rules.

questions.title: Why does `COPY main.c /src/` fail when you pipe in the Dockerfile?
questions.description: You run `docker build - < Dockerfile` from a directory that contains `main.c`.

options.text: The build gets only the Dockerfile text and no files, so `main.c` isn't available
Builds from standard input reject every `COPY`, even `COPY --from`
`-` makes the root directory `/` the context
With standard input, Docker requires source files to be executable

questions.explanation: With `-`, Docker reads standard input as the Dockerfile and sends no files with it. The current directory isn't the context, so the builder can't see `main.c`, even though it's on your machine.

questions.title: Does touching a copied file invalidate its build cache?
questions.description: Before a rebuild, only the modification time of `app.js` changes. Its content, permissions, ownership, and size stay the same. The Dockerfile has `COPY app.js /app/app.js`.

images.alt: Two Dockerfiles side by side. The first copies source before installing: FROM, COPY . /app, RUN npm ci. Any file edit invalidates the COPY layer and every layer after it, so the install reruns on every build. The second copies dependencies first: FROM, COPY package*.json, RUN npm ci, then COPY . /app. A source edit invalidates only the last layer, and the install stays cached until a manifest changes. Four cards follow. A COPY's cache key is the file's content plus metadata such as mode and ownership, so changing only its modification time invalidates nothing. A RUN's cache key is the command string alone, so a lone apt-get update matches last week's and reuses a stale index. --mount=type=secret keeps the value out of both the image and the cache key, so rotating a secret does not invalidate that step. --mount=type=cache needs BuildKit and never becomes part of the image.
images.caption: Content and metadata count. A new modification time alone doesn't.

options.text: Yes. Any newer modification time forces `COPY` and all later instructions to run
No. Docker leaves modification time out of the cache checksum
Only if the modification time changes by more than one second
Only remote builders ignore modification time

questions.explanation: For `ADD`, `COPY`, and `RUN` bind mounts, Docker checksums each file's content and metadata but skips `mtime`. Touching the file changes nothing Docker checks, so the cache still hits. Editing the content or changing other metadata, such as permissions, would invalidate it.

questions.title: Which changes can invalidate the cache for `COPY package.json /app/`?
questions.description: Select every change that can affect Docker's checksum for this file.

images.alt: Two Dockerfiles side by side. The first copies source before installing: FROM, COPY . /app, RUN npm ci. Any file edit invalidates the COPY layer and every layer after it, so the install reruns on every build. The second copies dependencies first: FROM, COPY package*.json, RUN npm ci, then COPY . /app. A source edit invalidates only the last layer, and the install stays cached until a manifest changes. Four cards follow. A COPY's cache key is the file's content plus metadata such as mode and ownership, so changing only its modification time invalidates nothing. A RUN's cache key is the command string alone, so a lone apt-get update matches last week's and reuses a stale index. --mount=type=secret keeps the value out of both the image and the cache key, so rotating a secret does not invalidate that step. --mount=type=cache needs BuildKit and never becomes part of the image.
images.caption: The `COPY` card lists what counts.

options.text: Changing the contents of `package.json`
Changing its metadata, such as permissions
Changing only the file's modification time
Changing an unrelated file that `.dockerignore` excludes

questions.explanation: Docker checksums only the files that `COPY` uses. Changing their content or metadata, such as permissions, changes the checksum. Changing only the modification time doesn't. An ignored file has no effect because the builder never receives it.

[Docker Docs: Build cache invalidation](https://docs.docker.com/build/cache/invalidation/)

[Docker Docs: Using the build cache](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/building-images/using-the-build-cache/)

questions.title: Why can `RUN apt-get update` return week-old data during a rebuild?

images.alt: Two Dockerfiles side by side. The first copies source before installing: FROM, COPY . /app, RUN npm ci. Any file edit invalidates the COPY layer and every layer after it, so the install reruns on every build. The second copies dependencies first: FROM, COPY package*.json, RUN npm ci, then COPY . /app. A source edit invalidates only the last layer, and the install stays cached until a manifest changes. Four cards follow. A COPY's cache key is the file's content plus metadata such as mode and ownership, so changing only its modification time invalidates nothing. A RUN's cache key is the command string alone, so a lone apt-get update matches last week's and reuses a stale index. --mount=type=secret keeps the value out of both the image and the cache key, so rotating a secret does not invalidate that step. --mount=type=cache needs BuildKit and never becomes part of the image.
images.caption: The cache key is the command string, so an unchanged command reuses the old result.

options.text: Docker checks the package repository only when the base image tag changes
Docker reuses the cached `RUN` result without checking whether remote package data changed
Docker freezes network access for all cached Dockerfiles
Package managers roll their index back to the image's creation date

questions.explanation: Docker never contacts the package repository when it checks the cache. If the command and the layers before it still match, Docker reuses last week's result. To make the step run again, use `--no-cache` or `--no-cache-filter`, or change an earlier layer.

questions.title: Which Dockerfile order keeps dependencies cached when you edit source code?
questions.description: It's a Node project, and `package.json` and `package-lock.json` define its dependencies.

images.alt: Two Dockerfiles side by side. The first copies source before installing: FROM, COPY . /app, RUN npm ci. Any file edit invalidates the COPY layer and every layer after it, so the install reruns on every build. The second copies dependencies first: FROM, COPY package*.json, RUN npm ci, then COPY . /app. A source edit invalidates only the last layer, and the install stays cached until a manifest changes. Four cards follow. A COPY's cache key is the file's content plus metadata such as mode and ownership, so changing only its modification time invalidates nothing. A RUN's cache key is the command string alone, so a lone apt-get update matches last week's and reuses a stale index. --mount=type=secret keeps the value out of both the image and the cache key, so rotating a secret does not invalidate that step. --mount=type=cache needs BuildKit and never becomes part of the image.
images.caption: The green Dockerfile copies the manifests before the source.

options.text: Copy all source, install dependencies, then copy the manifests again
Copy the manifests, install dependencies, then copy the rest of the source
Install dependencies before copying any manifests
Install dependencies, then copy the manifests and source in separate steps

questions.explanation: When a layer changes, Docker rebuilds every layer after it. Copy the package files and install dependencies first, then copy the source. A source edit rebuilds only the layers after the install, and a dependency change still reruns the install.
questions.references: [Docker Docs: Optimize cache usage: order your layers](https://docs.docker.com/build/cache/optimize/#order-your-layers)

questions.title: What must be true of a build that uses `RUN --mount=type=cache`?
questions.description: A package manager uses a cache mount to keep downloaded packages between builds.

images.alt: Two Dockerfiles side by side. The first copies source before installing: FROM, COPY . /app, RUN npm ci. Any file edit invalidates the COPY layer and every layer after it, so the install reruns on every build. The second copies dependencies first: FROM, COPY package*.json, RUN npm ci, then COPY . /app. A source edit invalidates only the last layer, and the install stays cached until a manifest changes. Four cards follow. A COPY's cache key is the file's content plus metadata such as mode and ownership, so changing only its modification time invalidates nothing. A RUN's cache key is the command string alone, so a lone apt-get update matches last week's and reuses a stale index. --mount=type=secret keeps the value out of both the image and the cache key, so rotating a secret does not invalidate that step. --mount=type=cache needs BuildKit and never becomes part of the image.
images.caption: It needs BuildKit and never becomes part of the image.

options.text: The final image contains the cache directory as the build saw it
The build must work with any cache contents, including an empty cache
Every build gets an immutable snapshot of the cache
Only the build that created a cache mount can read it

questions.explanation: A cache mount keeps downloads between builds, but Docker may overwrite or garbage-collect its contents. Write the step so it works with an empty or unexpected cache. Files in the cache mount don't end up in the `RUN` layer.

[Docker Docs: Optimize cache usage: cache mounts](https://docs.docker.com/build/cache/optimize/#use-cache-mounts)

questions.title: How should you pass a private registry token to one build step?

images.alt: Two Dockerfiles side by side. The first copies source before installing: FROM, COPY . /app, RUN npm ci. Any file edit invalidates the COPY layer and every layer after it, so the install reruns on every build. The second copies dependencies first: FROM, COPY package*.json, RUN npm ci, then COPY . /app. A source edit invalidates only the last layer, and the install stays cached until a manifest changes. Four cards follow. A COPY's cache key is the file's content plus metadata such as mode and ownership, so changing only its modification time invalidates nothing. A RUN's cache key is the command string alone, so a lone apt-get update matches last week's and reuses a stale index. --mount=type=secret keeps the value out of both the image and the cache key, so rotating a secret does not invalidate that step. --mount=type=cache needs BuildKit and never becomes part of the image.
images.caption: Only the secret mount leaves nothing in the image.

options.text: Declare it with `ARG TOKEN` and pass `--build-arg TOKEN=...`
Declare it with `ENV TOKEN=...` and unset it in a later layer
Pass it with `docker build --secret` and consume it using `RUN --mount=type=secret`
Copy it into the image and delete it before `CMD`

questions.explanation: `ARG` and `ENV` can leave the token in the final image, its metadata, or its history. A secret mount makes the token available only while that one `RUN` step runs, and Docker never writes it to the image layer.

questions.title: Does rotating a build secret invalidate the cache for the `RUN` step that uses it?

images.alt: Two Dockerfiles side by side. The first copies source before installing: FROM, COPY . /app, RUN npm ci. Any file edit invalidates the COPY layer and every layer after it, so the install reruns on every build. The second copies dependencies first: FROM, COPY package*.json, RUN npm ci, then COPY . /app. A source edit invalidates only the last layer, and the install stays cached until a manifest changes. Four cards follow. A COPY's cache key is the file's content plus metadata such as mode and ownership, so changing only its modification time invalidates nothing. A RUN's cache key is the command string alone, so a lone apt-get update matches last week's and reuses a stale index. --mount=type=secret keeps the value out of both the image and the cache key, so rotating a secret does not invalidate that step. --mount=type=cache needs BuildKit and never becomes part of the image.
images.caption: The secret value stays out of the image and out of the cache key.

options.text: Yes. Secret contents always become part of the layer checksum
No. Docker ignores the secret value but includes the secret ID and mount path
Only secrets longer than 32 bytes invalidate the cache
No. Neither the secret value nor its mount settings affect caching

questions.explanation: Docker leaves the secret's value out of the cache checksum, so a new value alone can still hit the cache. The secret ID and mount path are part of the checksum. If the step must rerun after a rotation, change a build argument that acts as a cache buster.

questions.title: Which build-stage files end up in the final image?
questions.description: A `build` stage has a compiler, the source tree, a package cache, and `/out/server`. A separate runtime stage runs `COPY --from=build /out/server /server`.

options.text: Every build-stage layer plus a marker hiding the compiler
Only the runtime stage's base image and what that stage adds, such as `/server`
The compiler and source tree, but not the package cache
Nothing from the build stage because stages cannot exchange files

questions.explanation: Each `FROM` starts a new stage. The runtime stage gets only its base image and what its own instructions add, including `/server` from `COPY --from=build`. The compiler, source tree, and package cache stay behind in the build stage.

questions.title: Which image does `docker build --target test .` produce?

options.text: An image of the `test` stage, without going on to the final stage
Only the individual instruction labeled `test`
The final image, with tests disabled
All stages merged into a single filesystem

questions.explanation: `--target test` stops the build at the `test` stage and outputs that image. BuildKit builds the stage and the stages it depends on, and can skip unrelated ones. One Dockerfile can then produce separate test, debug, and runtime images.
questions.references:
[Docker Docs: Stop at a specific build stage](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/#stop-at-a-specific-build-stage)

[Docker Docs: BuildKit stage dependency differences](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/#differences-between-legacy-builder-and-buildkit)

questions.title: Why does deleting a 200 MB archive in a later `RUN` still leave the image about 200 MB bigger?
questions.description: One `RUN` downloads `/tmp/sdk.tar`, and a later `RUN` deletes it.

images.alt: A stack of four read-only image layers: FROM node:22-slim, COPY package.json, RUN npm ci, and COPY . /app. On top is one thin read-write layer that belongs to a single container. Notes explain that writing to a file from the image first copies it up into the top layer and leaves the layer beneath unchanged; that changing one byte of a huge file makes OverlayFS copy the whole file up; that deleting something in a later RUN only records a whiteout while the earlier layer keeps the bytes; and that removing the container removes its writable layer. Three cards cover the other storage options. A named volume outlives its container and, when empty, is filled from the image directory. A bind mount hides whatever the image had at that path and is read-write by default. A tmpfs mount is kept in host memory and disappears when the container stops.
images.caption: A whiteout hides the file, and its bytes stay in the earlier layer.

options.text: The delete hides the file, but its bytes stay in the earlier, immutable layer
Docker compresses deleted files only after the container starts
Files under `/tmp` always count twice in image size
`RUN rm` changes image metadata but never the filesystem

questions.explanation: Image layers never change once built. The later `RUN` only hides the archive in the merged filesystem. Its bytes stay in the earlier layer and still count toward the image size. Download and delete temporary files in the same `RUN`, or do the work in a build stage that the final image doesn't use.

questions.title: Where does a container's write to `/etc/app.conf` go when the file came from the image?

images.alt: A stack of four read-only image layers: FROM node:22-slim, COPY package.json, RUN npm ci, and COPY . /app. On top is one thin read-write layer that belongs to a single container. Notes explain that writing to a file from the image first copies it up into the top layer and leaves the layer beneath unchanged; that changing one byte of a huge file makes OverlayFS copy the whole file up; that deleting something in a later RUN only records a whiteout while the earlier layer keeps the bytes; and that removing the container removes its writable layer. Three cards cover the other storage options. A named volume outlives its container and, when empty, is filled from the image directory. A bind mount hides whatever the image had at that path and is read-write by default. A tmpfs mount is kept in host memory and disappears when the container stops.
images.caption: The file is copied up into the container's layer. The image layer doesn't change.

options.text: Directly into the image's newest read-only layer
Into that container's thin writable layer, leaving the shared image layers unchanged
Into every container created from the same image
Into a volume that Docker creates automatically for every path

questions.explanation: Each container gets its own writable layer on top of the image. The change goes into that layer, so other containers still see the original file. When Docker removes the container, it removes the writable layer too.
questions.references:
[Docker Docs: Understanding image layers](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/building-images/understanding-image-layers/)

[Docker Docs: Storage drivers: containers and layers](https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/drivers/#container-and-layers)

questions.title: What happens the first time a container on OverlayFS changes one byte of a large image file?

images.alt: A stack of four read-only image layers: FROM node:22-slim, COPY package.json, RUN npm ci, and COPY . /app. On top is one thin read-write layer that belongs to a single container. Notes explain that writing to a file from the image first copies it up into the top layer and leaves the layer beneath unchanged; that changing one byte of a huge file makes OverlayFS copy the whole file up; that deleting something in a later RUN only records a whiteout while the earlier layer keeps the bytes; and that removing the container removes its writable layer. Three cards cover the other storage options. A named volume outlives its container and, when empty, is filled from the image directory. A bind mount hides whatever the image had at that path and is read-write by default. A tmpfs mount is kept in host memory and disappears when the container stops.
images.caption: Copy-up copies whole files.

options.text: OverlayFS copies the whole file into the writable layer before modifying the copy
Only the changed byte is stored, because OverlayFS always copies at block granularity
The lower image layer becomes writable for that container
OverlayFS rejects the change unless the file is on a named volume

questions.explanation: With the `overlay2` storage driver, the first write to an image file triggers `copy_up`. OverlayFS copies the whole file into the writable layer, then edits the copy. Because copy-up works on whole files, a one-byte edit can mean copying a large file. Later writes go to the copy.
questions.references: [Docker Docs: OverlayFS: writing to a file for the first time](https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/drivers/overlayfs-driver/#writing-to-a-file-for-the-first-time)

questions.title: Which image reference pulls the same image every time?

options.text: `ubuntu:latest`
`ubuntu:24.04`
`ubuntu@sha256:<exact-digest>`
`ubuntu` without a tag

questions.explanation: A publisher can move any tag, including a version tag like `24.04`, to a newer image. A digest identifies exact content, so pulling by digest gets the same image every time. The catch is that you get a newer image or security fixes only when you update the digest yourself.

questions.title: Why might `ENTRYPOINT node server.js` hide Docker's stop signal from Node?

options.text: Shell form runs through `/bin/sh -c`, so the shell can stay PID 1 with Node as its child
Node processes cannot receive Unix signals in containers
`ENTRYPOINT` disables signals unless an `EXPOSE` instruction is present
Docker sends stop signals only to programs started by `CMD`

questions.explanation: In shell form, Docker starts `/bin/sh -c`, so the shell can be PID 1 with Node running as its child. The shell may not pass Docker's stop signal on to Node. Exec form, `ENTRYPOINT ["node", "server.js"]`, makes Node the main process. If you use a wrapper script, it must forward signals, and it should start the application with `exec`.

questions.title: What does `docker stop` do when the main process does not exit during its grace period?

options.text: It pauses the container indefinitely
It sends the stop signal, `SIGTERM` by default, waits, then sends `SIGKILL`
It immediately sends `SIGKILL` and never waits
It sends `SIGINT` repeatedly until every process exits

questions.explanation: Docker sends the stop signal, `SIGTERM` by default, to the main process. If the process is still running when the timeout ends, Docker sends `SIGKILL`, which the process can't catch to clean up. You can change the signal with `STOPSIGNAL` or `--stop-signal`, and the wait with a timeout setting.

questions.title: By default, how many seconds does Docker wait before killing an unresponsive Linux container?
questions.description: Neither the container nor the command sets a stop timeout. Enter the number of seconds.
questions.explanation: By default, Docker waits 10 seconds for a Linux container and 30 seconds for a Windows container, then sends `SIGKILL` if the process is still running. A timeout of `-1` makes Docker wait with no deadline.

questions.title: Why would you use `docker run --init`?

options.text: It inserts a small PID 1 that forwards signals and reaps zombie processes
It rebuilds the image before every container start
It gives the container a private kernel
It waits for every declared network port to become healthy

questions.explanation: On Linux, PID 1 has special duties, such as reaping zombie processes. `--init` runs a small init process as PID 1 to handle them, and a default Docker install uses `tini` for it. Docker's Compose docs note that this init process also forwards signals.

questions.title: What does `EXPOSE 8080` do by itself?

options.text: It opens host port 8080 to the public internet
It records container port 8080 in the image but does not publish a host port
It forces the application to listen on port 8080
It creates a user-defined bridge network named `8080`

questions.explanation: `EXPOSE` records which port the application is expected to use. It doesn't start a listener or map a host port. To publish, use `-p` for a mapping you choose, or `-P` to map every exposed port to a random high host port.

questions.title: Where does traffic to host port 8080 go with `docker run -p 8080:80 nginx`?

options.text: To TCP port 80 inside the container
To TCP port 8080 inside the container
To host port 80 after passing through container port 8080
Nowhere unless the Dockerfile also says `EXPOSE 8080`

questions.explanation: The format is `HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT`, so Docker forwards connections from host port 8080 to TCP port 80 in the container. An explicit `-p` mapping works even when the Dockerfile has no matching `EXPOSE`.

questions.title: Who can reach a port published with `-p 8080:80` and no host IP?

options.text: Only processes on the Docker host
Anyone who can reach one of the host's network interfaces, if firewalls and routing allow it
Only containers on the same bridge
Only the user who launched the container

questions.explanation: Without a host IP, Docker publishes the port on every host address, so other machines may be able to reach it. If only the Docker host should connect, bind to loopback with `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80`. Add the matching IPv6 loopback mapping if you need it.

questions.title: How should `web` connect to `db` on the same user-defined bridge?

options.text: Use `db` as the hostname and the database's container port
Use `localhost` because both containers share loopback
Use the Docker host's published database port in every case
Read the database container's IP once and hard-code it

questions.explanation: A user-defined bridge has built-in DNS for container names and aliases. `web` can connect to `db` on the database's container port, and you don't need to publish that port on the host. A hard-coded IP breaks when Docker recreates `db` with a new address. The name keeps working.

questions.title: What does `localhost` mean inside the `web` container?
questions.description: A database runs in a separate `db` container on the same user-defined network.

options.text: The `web` container's own loopback interface
The Docker host
Whichever container started most recently
Every container attached to the bridge

questions.explanation: Each container has its own network stack with its own loopback interface. Inside `web`, `localhost` is `web` itself. To reach the database, use the hostname `db`.

questions.title: Do you need to publish a database port so another container on the same user-defined bridge can reach it?
questions.description: Assume the database listens on its container network interface.

options.text: Yes. Every container-to-container connection must go through a host port
No. Containers on the same user-defined bridge can connect directly
Yes, unless both containers use the same image
No, but peers can reach only the ports listed in `EXPOSE`

questions.explanation: Containers on the same user-defined bridge can connect to each other's ports directly. Publishing is for traffic that comes through the host or, under the default bridge rules, from other networks. Peers on the same network don't need it, and `EXPOSE` doesn't filter their traffic.

questions.title: What happens to a named volume after the container using it is removed?

images.alt: A stack of four read-only image layers: FROM node:22-slim, COPY package.json, RUN npm ci, and COPY . /app. On top is one thin read-write layer that belongs to a single container. Notes explain that writing to a file from the image first copies it up into the top layer and leaves the layer beneath unchanged; that changing one byte of a huge file makes OverlayFS copy the whole file up; that deleting something in a later RUN only records a whiteout while the earlier layer keeps the bytes; and that removing the container removes its writable layer. Three cards cover the other storage options. A named volume outlives its container and, when empty, is filled from the image directory. A bind mount hides whatever the image had at that path and is read-write by default. A tmpfs mount is kept in host memory and disappears when the container stops.
images.caption: The left-hand card shows that a volume outlives its container.

options.text: It persists independently until the volume itself is removed
It is copied back into the image
It is always deleted with the container
It survives only while another container is running

questions.explanation: A volume has its own lifecycle. Removing a container doesn't remove a named volume, even when `docker rm --volumes` cleans up the container's anonymous volumes. A new container can mount the same named volume and read its data.

questions.title: What's in a new, empty volume when you mount it over an image directory that has files?
questions.description: The image contains `/app/defaults/config.ini`. You mount a new, empty volume at `/app/defaults` with default options.

images.alt: A stack of four read-only image layers: FROM node:22-slim, COPY package.json, RUN npm ci, and COPY . /app. On top is one thin read-write layer that belongs to a single container. Notes explain that writing to a file from the image first copies it up into the top layer and leaves the layer beneath unchanged; that changing one byte of a huge file makes OverlayFS copy the whole file up; that deleting something in a later RUN only records a whiteout while the earlier layer keeps the bytes; and that removing the container removes its writable layer. Three cards cover the other storage options. A named volume outlives its container and, when empty, is filled from the image directory. A bind mount hides whatever the image had at that path and is read-write by default. A tmpfs mount is kept in host memory and disappears when the container stops.
images.caption: Docker fills an empty volume from the directory it covers.

options.text: Docker copies the image's files into the volume, so `config.ini` is there
The directory is empty because mounts always discard image content
The volume contains a symbolic link to the image layer
Container creation fails because the target directory isn't empty

questions.explanation: By default, Docker copies the files already at the mount target into a new, empty volume, so the volume gets `config.ini`. Add `volume-nocopy` if you want the volume to stay empty.
questions.references: [Docker Docs: Mounting a volume over existing data](https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/volumes/#mounting-a-volume-over-existing-data)

questions.title: What does a default read-write bind mount over `/app` do?
questions.description: The image already has files in `/app`, and you bind-mount the host directory `/work/source` there. Select every correct statement.

images.alt: A stack of four read-only image layers: FROM node:22-slim, COPY package.json, RUN npm ci, and COPY . /app. On top is one thin read-write layer that belongs to a single container. Notes explain that writing to a file from the image first copies it up into the top layer and leaves the layer beneath unchanged; that changing one byte of a huge file makes OverlayFS copy the whole file up; that deleting something in a later RUN only records a whiteout while the earlier layer keeps the bytes; and that removing the container removes its writable layer. Three cards cover the other storage options. A named volume outlives its container and, when empty, is filled from the image directory. A bind mount hides whatever the image had at that path and is read-write by default. A tmpfs mount is kept in host memory and disappears when the container stops.
images.caption: The host directory hides the image's files while it's mounted.

options.text: The mount hides the image's original `/app` files while it's in place
Container processes can modify files in `/work/source` because bind mounts are writable by default
Docker permanently deletes the hidden `/app` files from the image's layers
Docker copies `/work/source` into a daemon-managed volume before the container starts

questions.explanation: The bind mount hides the image's `/app` files while it's mounted, and they're still in the image afterward. Bind mounts are writable by default, so the container can change files in `/work/source` on your host. Add `readonly` or `ro` when the container only needs to read.

questions.title: What happens to files in a Docker `tmpfs` mount when the container stops?

images.alt: A stack of four read-only image layers: FROM node:22-slim, COPY package.json, RUN npm ci, and COPY . /app. On top is one thin read-write layer that belongs to a single container. Notes explain that writing to a file from the image first copies it up into the top layer and leaves the layer beneath unchanged; that changing one byte of a huge file makes OverlayFS copy the whole file up; that deleting something in a later RUN only records a whiteout while the earlier layer keeps the bytes; and that removing the container removes its writable layer. Three cards cover the other storage options. A named volume outlives its container and, when empty, is filled from the image directory. A bind mount hides whatever the image had at that path and is read-write by default. A tmpfs mount is kept in host memory and disappears when the container stops.
images.caption: The data is in memory and disappears when the container stops.

options.text: Docker commits them into a new image layer
They disappear with the mount and don't persist
They move automatically into a named volume
They stay in host RAM until Docker is uninstalled

questions.explanation: Docker removes a `tmpfs` mount when the container stops, and its files go with it. While the container runs, the data is in host memory, outside the container's writable layer. Linux can still swap tmpfs pages to disk, so don't count on `tmpfs` to keep data off disk.

questions.title: What happens to database files in a container's writable layer when you delete the container?

images.alt: A stack of four read-only image layers: FROM node:22-slim, COPY package.json, RUN npm ci, and COPY . /app. On top is one thin read-write layer that belongs to a single container. Notes explain that writing to a file from the image first copies it up into the top layer and leaves the layer beneath unchanged; that changing one byte of a huge file makes OverlayFS copy the whole file up; that deleting something in a later RUN only records a whiteout while the earlier layer keeps the bytes; and that removing the container removes its writable layer. Three cards cover the other storage options. A named volume outlives its container and, when empty, is filled from the image directory. A bind mount hides whatever the image had at that path and is read-write by default. A tmpfs mount is kept in host memory and disappears when the container stops.
images.caption: Deleting the container deletes its top layer.

options.text: The next container from the same image tag can use them
They're gone, along with the container's writable layer
Docker pushes them to the registry with the image
Docker turns them into an anonymous volume

questions.explanation: Each container has its own writable layer. Stopping the container keeps the layer, and deleting the container removes it. Keep data that must survive, or that gets written a lot, in a volume or another storage system.

questions.title: Which statements about default Linux container isolation are true?
questions.description: Select every true statement about ordinary Docker Engine containers. Ignore the extra VM that Docker Desktop adds.

options.text: Namespaces give each container its own view of resources such as processes and networks
Containers share the host's Linux kernel instead of booting their own
A container is as strong a boundary as a hardware virtual machine
Root inside a container always has unrestricted root access to the host

questions.explanation: Namespaces give a container its own view of processes, networks, and other resources, and cgroups track and limit what it uses. Every container still runs on the host kernel. Capabilities and seccomp limit what container processes can do. How strong the boundary is depends on the container's configuration and the host kernel, so treat it differently from a VM with its own kernel.
questions.references:
[Docker Docs: Docker Engine security](https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/)

[Docker Docs: Isolation layers: containers share the host kernel](https://docs.docker.com/ai/sandboxes/security/isolation/)

questions.title: Without resource limits, how much CPU and memory can a container use?

options.text: At most one CPU and 512 MB of memory
As much as the host kernel scheduler and available resources allow
An equal, fixed share of the host for each running container
None until you set `--cpus` and `--memory`

questions.explanation: By default, Docker sets no hard CPU or memory limit. A container can use as much as the host kernel allows, which can starve other workloads or make the kernel start killing processes when memory runs out. Set cgroup limits with flags such as `--cpus` and `--memory`.

questions.title: With these limits, how many megabytes of swap can the container use?
questions.description: The container starts with `--memory=300m --memory-swap=600m`. Enter only the swap amount in megabytes.
questions.explanation: `--memory-swap` is the total of memory plus swap, not swap alone. Subtract the 300 MB memory limit from the 600 MB total: `600 - 300 = 300`. The container can use 300 MB of swap.

questions.title: What does Docker's default seccomp profile do on a supported Linux host?

options.text: It blocks selected system calls to shrink the kernel's attack surface, while common workloads still run
It gives each container a separate Linux kernel
It encrypts all container filesystem layers
It publishes only ports named by `EXPOSE`

questions.explanation: Seccomp is a Linux kernel feature that restricts which system calls a process can make. Docker applies its default profile whenever the host supports seccomp, unless you pass a different profile. It works alongside namespaces, capabilities, and cgroups, and the container still shares the host kernel.
